questions.question_text: Changes seen in normal ageing.

options.text: Background slowing and diffuse superimposed beta activity
Focal and generalized spikes, sharp waves, polyspikes and spike–wave complexes
Generalized slowing of alpha rhythm, diffuse theta and delta activity with decline of low-voltage beta activity and focal delta activity in temporal areas
Non-specific slow waves and irregular high-voltage delta activity

correct_answer.text: Generalized slowing of alpha rhythm, diffuse theta and delta activity with decline of low-voltage beta activity and focal delta activity in temporal areas

correct_answers.text: Generalized slowing of alpha rhythm, diffuse theta and delta activity with decline of low-voltage beta activity and focal delta activity in temporal areas

questions.explanation: In normal ageing (after the age of 60 years), there is generalized slowing of alpha rhythm, diffuse theta and delta activity with decline of low-voltage beta activity and focal delta activity in temporal areas.

questions.question_text: A 75-year-old man presents with confusion, disorientation and visual hallucinations. He has been complaining of a burning sensation on passing urine and having fever for the past few days.

options.text: Background slowing and diffuse superimposed beta activity
Focal and generalized spikes, sharp waves, polyspikes and spike–wave complexes
Generalized slowing of alpha rhythm, diffuse theta and delta activity with decline of low-voltage beta activity and focal delta activity in temporal areas
Non-specific slow waves and irregular high-voltage delta activity

correct_answer.text: Non-specific slow waves and irregular high-voltage delta activity

correct_answers.text: Non-specific slow waves and irregular high-voltage delta activity

questions.explanation: This man is suffering from delirium, and the EEG is most likely to show diffuse non-specific slowing. Delta activity, asymmetry in delta waves and localized spike–wave complexes occur more frequently in those with intracranial pathology. Alpha activity correlates with cognitive functioning, and delta activity correlates with length of illness.

questions.question_text: A 62-year-old woman has been going to various doctors to obtain sleeping pills. One day, she is found unconscious at home with several empty bottles of sleeping pills.

options.text: Background slowing and diffuse superimposed beta activity
Focal and generalized spikes, sharp waves, polyspikes and spike–wave complexes
Generalized slowing of alpha rhythm, diffuse theta and delta activity with decline of low-voltage beta activity and focal delta activity in temporal areas
Non-specific slow waves and irregular high-voltage delta activity

correct_answer.text: Background slowing and diffuse superimposed beta activity

correct_answers.text: Background slowing and diffuse superimposed beta activity

questions.explanation: This is most suggestive of benzodiazepine intoxication. In general, benzodiazepines cause background slowing and diffuse superimposed beta activity and sometimes decreased alpha activity.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man with a background history of epilepsy is sent to the hospital after being found lying on the floor with jerking movements and urinary incontinence. He has no recollection what happened before the incident.

options.text: Background slowing and diffuse superimposed beta activity
Focal and generalized spikes, sharp waves, polyspikes and spike–wave complexes
Generalized slowing of alpha rhythm, diffuse theta and delta activity with decline of low-voltage beta activity and focal delta activity in temporal areas
Non-specific slow waves and irregular high-voltage delta activity

correct_answer.text: Focal and generalized spikes, sharp waves, polyspikes and spike–wave complexes

correct_answers.text: Focal and generalized spikes, sharp waves, polyspikes and spike–wave complexes

questions.explanation: This is most suggestive of epilepsy. Focal and generalized spikes, sharp waves, polyspikes and spike–wave complexes are typical features of an EEG seen in epilepsy.

questions.question_text: Approximately 25% of cases of schizophrenia show good clinical and social recovery. Which of the above factors is indicative of a good prognosis?

options.text: Short duration of illness prior to treatment

questions.explanation: Schizophrenia is considered to be a heterogeneous disorder, and there are no completely reliable predictors of outcome. Approximately 25% of cases of schizophrenia show good clinical and social recovery. Factors associated with a good prognosis include female gender, being married, good premorbid social adjustment, family history of affective disorder, short duration of illness prior to treatment, no ventricular enlargement, abrupt onset of illness, late onset of illness, having an affective component, paranoid ideation, lack of negative symptoms, lack of cognitive impairment and good initial response to treatment.

questions.question_text: In renal impairment, It has been noted that fewer than half of patients have poor long-term outcome. Which of the following factors is associated with poor prognosis?

options.text: Short duration of illness prior to treatment

questions.explanation: Schizophrenia is considered to be a heterogeneous disorder, and there are no completely reliable predictors of outcome. Fewer than half of patients have poor long-term outcome. Factors associated with a poor prognosis include male gender, family history of psychosis and ventricular enlargement.

questions.question_text: In renal impairment, Which antipsychotics can be used?
questions.explanation: Haloperidol of dosage between 2 and 6 mg per day can be used. Olanzapine at 5 mg per day can also be used.

questions.question_text: In renal impairment, Which antidepressants can be used?
questions.explanation: Citalopram and sertraline are indicated for usage in patients with renal impairment and depressive disorder. Tricyclic antidepressants are not indicated, largely due to their anticholinergic side effects.

questions.question_text: In renal impairment, Which of the above mood stabilizers is contraindicated for usage?
questions.explanation: Valproate, carbamazepine and lamotrigine can be used for patients with renal impairments. Lithium is contraindicated.

questions.question_text: A 3-year-old child presents with hepatosplenomegaly, hirustism, corneal clouding and recurrent respiratory infections. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is the classical presentation of this disorder. In addition, children may have short stature. The associated psychiatric features include anxiety and fearful feelings. There may be moderate-to-severe learning disabilities. There may be recurrent respiratory infections and death before the age of 10 years.

questions.question_text: A 16-year-old boy is referred to the psychiatrist because of self-harming, which includes biting of lips, inside of mouth and fingers. There is associated failure of secondary sexual development. His grandfather also suffered from the same disorder. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is the classical presentation of the disorder. In addition, there will associated errors in metabolism, thus resulting in the accumulation of uric acid. During infancy, orange uricosuric acid sand is found in the nappy. The child then develops hypotonia followed by spastic choreoathetosis, dysphagia and dysarthria. The age of onset of self-injurious behaviours is usually before the age of 3 years. Lips and fingers are often bitten.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old married man with history of mild learning disability is referred to you. His history suggests possible fertility problems. Physical examination shows gynaecomastia and small testes. There has not been any known family history of similar problems. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The classical clinical features are that newborn boys are usually normal. Sexual orientation is usually normal and results in heterosexual marriage. The child tends to be passive and compliant in childhood but more aggressive and antisocial past puberty.

questions.question_text: A 4-year-old child is referred to the psychiatrist for delayed speech and language. He was initially suspected to suffer from autism. He has gaze aversion and social avoidance. His IQ is 60. He also has attention deficit. Physical examination shows enlarged testes, large ears, long face and flat feet. Mental state examination reveals limited eye contact, perseveration of words, echolalia and stereotypical behaviour such as hand flapping. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of learning disability. It accounts for 10%–12% of mental retardation in men. It is an X-linked dominant genetic disorder with low penetrance.

questions.question_text: What is the percentage of mild learning disability patients suffering from epilepsy?
questions.explanation: For individuals diagnosed with mild learning disability, the estimated prevalence of epilepsy is that of 12%–18%.

questions.question_text: What is the percentage of severe learning disability patients suffering from epilepsy?
questions.explanation: Approximately 30%–37% of individuals diagnosed with severe mental retardation or learning disability do suffer from comorbid condition such as epilepsy.

The aggression is directed particularly at vulnerable people and pets at home. He does not have ADHD. He refuses psychotherapy, which his parents have also not found helpful.

options.text: Duty to inform the police if not reported yet
Obtain informed consent from the child and his or her parents

questions.explanation: Short-term risperidone (at a dose of 0.25–2 mg) can be used in adolescents with conduct disorder with aggressive behaviour who refuse psychological treatment.

questions.question_text: Your core trainee consults you, as she was requested by her GP to perform a psychiatric assessment on a 15-year-old boy who has been involved in shoplifting over a 3-month period.

options.text: Duty to inform the police if not reported yet
Obtain informed consent from the child and his or her parents

correct_answer.text: Duty to inform the police if not reported yet

correct_answers.text: Duty to inform the police if not reported yet
Obtain informed consent from the child and his or her parents

questions.explanation: This may be a case of juvenile delinquency with ethical, legal and clinical problems. Aetiological factors may include living in an inner city area, lack of caring supervision and lower socio-economic class. The trainee needs to obtain informed consent from the adolescent and parents and must also inform them about any legal obligations, such as duty to inform the police. Clinical assessment should address developmental stage, family reaction and psychiatric issues, while forensic assessment should evaluate the nature of offences, risk and awareness of consequences.

questions.question_text: A 15-year-old boy is referred for treatment by the children’s court. He recently lit a fire that resulted in significant damage to a shop. He was previously arrested for shoplifting and fighting. Previous history shows that he does not have learning disability or attention-deficit disorder.

options.text: Duty to inform the police if not reported yet
Obtain informed consent from the child and his or her parents

questions.explanation: This is a case of juvenile delinquency after excluding common causes for fire-setting in young people. Multisystemic therapy is the treatment of choice. It involves family therapy focusing on effective communication, systematic reward and punishment systems, problem-solving approaches to conflicts, peer involvement strategies and liaison with educational and social services.

questions.question_text: An 8-year-old child has frequent loss of temper, arguments with parents and feels irritable at home but not at school. The symptoms have persisted for 8 months. The parents are asking for help.

options.text: Duty to inform the police if not reported yet
Obtain informed consent from the child and his or her parents

questions.explanation: Family therapy and parent management training are both possible treatments for oppositional defiant disorder in children.

questions.question_text: If this is a case of incest, which family members may be involved?
questions.explanation: Incest is generally forbidden across cultures. In law, it is an offence for a man to have sexual intercourse with a woman he knows to be his daughter, granddaughter, mother, sister or half-sister. Sibling incest relationships are the most common, followed by father–daughter relationships.

questions.question_text: Which family member should not be invited to the family meeting?
questions.explanation: The alleged perpetrator (father) should not be invited to a supportive family meeting for the victim.

questions.question_text: The majority of abuse is committed by which family members?
questions.explanation: In childhood sexual abuse, the perpetrator is most often a parent, usually the father, but mothers can also be involved.

questions.question_text: She was diagnosed as suffering from Munchausen syndrome by proxy in the past. This syndrome is associated with psychological overdependence of which person on the child?
questions.explanation: Munchausen syndrome by proxy is typically perpetrated by the mother, who exhibits psychological overdependence on the child and fabricates or induces illness in the child.

questions.question_text: An 80-year-old man presents with fluctuating, progressive memory loss and emotional incontinence. He has a history of falls and is being treated for hypertension by his GP. His relatives say that his personality is preserved.
questions.explanation: Vascular dementia is characterized by a stepwise deteriorating course, focal neurological signs and evidence of cerebrovascular disease, while personality may be relatively preserved early on.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old woman presents with memory loss following the death of her husband 4 months ago. She also complains of poor sleep, lack of energy and weight loss. During the cognitive assessment, she is not keen to answer questions.
questions.explanation: In pseudodementia, cognitive deficits arise from depression. Onset is often acute, effort is poor during testing, patients answer 'don't know,' and memory deficits are reported more by the patient than by informants.

questions.question_text: A 75-year-old man presents with cognitive impairment, fluctuating levels of consciousness, particularly confusion and bizarre behaviour in the evenings. His daughter claims that he has been seeing ghosts and has not been able to turn in his bed. On physical examination, he is found to have hypertonia and hypersalivation. The MMSE score is 15/30. These above symptoms worsen following the commencement of antipsychotic medication.
questions.explanation: Lewy body dementia features fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonian signs and marked sensitivity to antipsychotics.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman presents with cognitive deterioration and mood changes. On physical examination, there are gait abnormalities. She has a medical history of epilepsy and migraines with aura. She also has episodes of left-sided muscular weakness. On further inquiry, you learn that her aunt also has similar problems.
questions.explanation: Cerebral autosomal-dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL) is caused by Notch3 mutations, leading to subcortical strokes, cognitive decline, mood changes and focal neurological deficits in a dominant inheritance pattern.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old woman was found wandering on the streets with some memory loss after the recent funeral of her husband. She was brought in by the police for psychiatric assessment. When you assess her, she is unable to recall her personal details. She is physically well, and all investigations are normal.
questions.explanation: Psychogenic fugue involves sudden, unexpected travel away from home with inability to recall one’s past, preserved personal identity skills, and normal physical and investigative findings.

questions.explanation: Under the McNaughton rule, a defendant who, by reason of mental disease, did not understand the nature or wrongness of the act at the time of offending is not guilty by reason of insanity.

options.text: Not guilty by reason of insanity (NGRI) or McNaughton rule

questions.explanation: A hospital order under the Mental Health Act is a disposal by the court as an alternative to imprisonment, often accompanied by a restriction order.

questions.question_text: A 68-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus and congestive heart failure on fluoxetine, metformin and furosemide complains of low mood and weight loss. Which is the most likely cause of her weight loss?
questions.explanation: Her weight loss is most consistent with an iatrogenic cause (furosemide), which can produce diuresis and unintentional weight loss.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old Irish woman with lethargy, frequent diarrhoea, offensive stools, weight loss, pallor, clubbing, abdominal distension and oral ulceration on iron and vitamin D supplements has an abnormal barium follow-through. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Her presentation and investigation (offensive, steatorrhoea stools; iron deficiency; positive barium follow-through) are most consistent with coeliac disease.

questions.question_text: A 16-year-old girl admitted with fever, weight loss, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, clubbing, aphthous ulceration, perianal skin tags, is a smoker and is nil by mouth. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Her age, smoking history, perianal tags, mouth ulcers and inflammatory symptoms are most consistent with Crohn’s disease.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man with migratory polyarthritis, weight loss, clubbing, pigmentation on sulphamethoxazole-trimethoprim has eosinophilic inclusions on jejunal biopsy. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Whipple’s disease presents with migratory arthritis, weight loss, malabsorption, pigmentation changes and PAS-positive macrophages in the jejunal biopsy.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old university student has been having a gradual deterioration in his academic performance. He is currently withdrawn and does not spend time as he used to with his peers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Simple schizophrenia features an insidious onset of negative symptoms (withdrawal, apathy) without prominent positive symptoms.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old university student diagnosed with schizophrenia is compliant with medications for one year and has minimal residual positive symptoms. He now presents with a 4-week history of low mood, poor sleep and appetite. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Post-schizophrenia depression occurs when depressive symptoms emerge in a patient with previously stabilized schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: An 18-year-old girl who has always been shy and introverted presents with marked affective changes and fragmentary delusions. What is the most likely subtype of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Hebephrenic (disorganized) schizophrenia is characterized by disorganized thought, affective changes and fragmentary delusions.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old mother 6 months postpartum has poor sleep, weight loss, tiredness, morning guilt, checking her baby every 5 minutes and excess worry about harm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: She meets criteria for a depressive episode with postpartum onset; her obsessive checking is secondary to her depression and anxiety.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old unemployed man was arrested for dangerous driving at 120 km/h believing paparazzi were harming him, has grandiose plans to pursue a PhD and advises the Prime Minister on investments. He has a ten-year history of psychiatric complications on antidepressants and claims he hears voices. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: His grandiosity, risky behaviour and decreased need for sleep are characteristic of a manic episode in bipolar disorder.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man firmly believes his gut has rotted and he is dead, ceases eating or drinking. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A nihilistic delusion of bodily decay with refusal to eat or drink is typical of psychotic depression (Cotard’s syndrome).

questions.question_text: A man passed over for promotion does not get upset at work but loses his temper at another driver on the way home.
questions.explanation: Displacement involves transferring emotional reactions from the true object to a less threatening substitute.

questions.question_text: He denies his anger toward his boss, saying “She’s like a mother to me – always kind and supportive.”
questions.explanation: Denial involves refusing to acknowledge an uncomfortable reality or emotion.

questions.question_text: He suggests that his anger is due to his childhood and then begins to speak about all the books he has recently read on child-rearing across different cultures.
questions.explanation: Intellectualization involves focusing on abstract or intellectual details to avoid emotional distress.

questions.question_text: Alpha-synuclein cytoplasmic inclusions.
questions.explanation: Lewy body dementia is characterized by alpha-synuclein–positive intracytoplasmic inclusions (Lewy bodies) in cortical neurons.

questions.question_text: Glial cytoplasmic inclusion bodies.
questions.explanation: Shy–Drager syndrome (multiple system atrophy) shows glial cytoplasmic inclusions.

questions.question_text: Neurofibrillary tangles.
questions.explanation: Neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau are seen in Alzheimer’s disease and, to a lesser extent, in Lewy body dementia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following family members is typically involved in a case of incest?
questions.explanation: Incest typically involves first-degree relatives: father–child or siblings (elder or younger brother) relationships.

questions.question_text: Which family member should not be involved if a family meeting is conducted in a case of incest?
questions.explanation: The alleged perpetrator (father) should not be present at a supportive family meeting for the victim.

questions.question_text: The majority of abuse is usually committed by which family members?
questions.explanation: Most child sexual abuse is committed by parents—more often the father, but mothers can also be perpetrators.
